issues.legal_issue: Statements made by alleged conspirators after the conspiracy has ended cannot be used against another accused under the rule governing evidence of conspiracy.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on confessions made by two co-accused after the murder to implicate the applicant in a conspiracy.
The record contained no worthwhile prima facie evidence, apart from those confessions, that the applicant and the co-accused were parties to the conspiracy.
issues.conclusion: On the material before the Court at the bail stage, the conspiracy-evidence rule could not be used to support the prosecution’s reliance on those confessions against the applicant; the Court left the broader question for consideration at trial.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10 of the Evidence Act applies where prima facie evidence establishes a conspiracy, and then makes acts and statements in furtherance of the common intention relevant against conspirators. Under Mirza Akbar v. King Emperor, statements made after the common intention or conspiracy has ceased are not covered. The Court did not finally decide the question, given that this was a bail proceeding.

predicates.bail_application: A court is considering an accused person’s application for release on bail.
predicates.independent_prima_facie_conspiracy_evide: Evidence apart from the challenged statements provides an initial basis to believe that the accused participated in a conspiracy.
predicates.statements_made_after_conspiracy_ended: The challenged statements were made after the alleged conspiracy had ended.

issues.definition: When a bail application rests on post-conspiracy statements and there is no independent initial evidence of the accused’s participation, those statements are not used against other suspects under the conspiracy-evidence rule.

issues.legal_issue: A statement about possible responsibility for a person’s death is not admissible as a death-related statement unless it concerns the cause of death or a circumstance of the transaction resulting in death.
material_facts: Before his death, the deceased told a witness by telephone that a petition had been numbered and that the applicant alone would be responsible if any danger came to him.
The statement did not concern the cause of the deceased’s death or a circumstance of the transaction that resulted in his death.
issues.conclusion: The statement did not fall within the death-related exception in Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act and was inadmissible on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act covers a statement by a deceased person relating to the cause of death or to circumstances of the transaction resulting in death. The Court held that the statement described here did not meet that test.

predicates.deceased_made_statement: A person who later died made a statement before death.
predicates.statement_unrelated_to_cause_or_death_tr: The statement did not relate to the cause of death or a circumstance of the transaction resulting in death.

issues.definition: If, during a bail application, a deceased person’s statement is unrelated to the cause of death or the transaction resulting in death, the statement is inadmissible as a death-related statement.

issues.legal_issue: A decision on a later bail application involving repeated prior applications does not establish a universal rule for every bail application.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on a prior decision involving an accused who had made several earlier bail applications, most of which had been rejected.
The application before the Court was being considered for the first time by it.
issues.conclusion: The observations in the cited prior decision could not be applied as a general rule to every case, including this application.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 437 and 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and distinguished Kalyan Chandra Sarkar v. Rajesh Ranjan, which involved a different history of repeated bail applications. It noted that the considerations relevant to bail include the nature and seriousness of the offence, the character of the evidence, circumstances peculiar to the accused, the prospect of securing the accused’s attendance, the risk of witness tampering, and the interests of the public or the State; it also relied on State v. Capt. Jagjit Singh and Gurcharan Singh v. State (Delhi Administration).

predicates.application_considered_for_first_time: The application is being considered by the deciding court for the first time.
predicates.cited_case_involved_repeated_prior_appli: The cited decision arose from a case in which the accused had made several earlier bail applications.

issues.definition: When a court considers a bail application for the first time, a precedent arising from repeated earlier applications is not treated as a universal rule for deciding it.

issues.legal_issue: Bail is warranted where the material available at the bail stage does not make a sufficiently strong prima facie case against the accused.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on letters recovered from the deceased’s home, but there was no evidence that the applicant had received them or that he had shown resentment toward the deceased because of them.

The prosecution first alleged that money for the assailants had been withdrawn from a bank account, then advanced a different account of the money; bank records showed that the cash said to have been received had been deposited shortly afterwards.

The main statements directly implicating the applicant were confessions by co-accused, one of which was retracted, and the prosecution’s reliance on those statements under the conspiracy-evidence rule was unsupported by independent prima facie evidence of conspiracy.
The deceased’s telephone statement to a witness did not concern the cause of death or a circumstance of the transaction resulting in death.
The prosecution said the applicant had spoken to co-accused, but the material did not connect those calls to the alleged attackers or the persons said to have waited outside.

The prosecution referred to unidentified witnesses said to have heard the applicant direct co-accused to eliminate the deceased; the Court considered it improbable that such a conversation would have been held where strangers could hear it.
issues.conclusion: The Court found that a strong prima facie case had been made out for bail, allowed the appeal, set aside the order refusing bail, and directed release subject to conditions, including surrender of the applicant’s passport and not visiting the premises of the institution until the charge sheet was filed. Its observations were expressly limited to the bail application and were not a final opinion on the issues for trial.
issues.legal_principle: In deciding bail for a non-bailable offence, the Court considers the nature and seriousness of the offence, the character of the evidence, circumstances peculiar to the accused, the likelihood of securing the accused’s presence at trial, the risk of witness tampering, the larger interests of the public or the State, and other relevant circumstances. The Court relied on State v. Capt. Jagjit Singh and Gurcharan Singh v. State (Delhi Administration), and treated Kalyan Chandra Sarkar v. Rajesh Ranjan as confined to its own facts. Its assessment was only prima facie and did not determine guilt.
